implementation_notes: In TypeScript the registry comes from the framework: Angular's Injector.get(token) resolves providers declared in the DI system, with InjectionToken<T> supplying a runtime, typed key for interfaces and parameterised types, while NestJS exposes ModuleRef.get(token, { strict: false }) to pull a provider out of its module container. Tokens are identity-based and typed, which is the pattern done well - the compiler keeps token and resolved type in step even though resolution is a runtime act - and the failures stay runtime ones (NullInjectorError, "no provider for token"). Use the injector only in code the framework instantiates (legacy adapters, dynamic components, NestJS dynamic-module factories) and use constructor parameters or inject() everywhere else.
pitfalls: A token created twice with the same description is two different tokens: re-creating an InjectionToken in another module yields NullInjectorError with no hint about the duplicate.

Resolving inside service methods hides the graph from the framework's static analysis; prefer constructor parameters or inject() for classes the DI system creates and keep Injector.get for the framework-created ones.
NestJS rejects request-scoped providers in ModuleRef.get (use resolve(), which is async), so resolving the wrong way throws at run time rather than at build time.

variants.name: Hand-written registry keyed by typed tokens
variants.idiom_name: Map<symbol, unknown> behind Token<T> branded keys with register/resolve
variants.implementation_notes: Without a framework the same mechanism is a few lines: a registry keyed by typed tokens - an InjectionToken-like value carrying a phantom type parameter plus a unique symbol - with a register step at the composition root and a get<T>(token) that throws when the token is unknown. Making the token generic keeps call sites typed without decorators or reflect-metadata and works for pure functions and plain classes as well as for interfaces, which is what the framework version buys at the cost of a container. This is the honest choice for libraries that must not depend on a container and for tests that need to swap exactly one binding.
pitfalls: The __type member is phantom: nothing stops registering a value of the wrong type for a token, so add a runtime shape check (or a brand validation) at registration where correctness matters.
A module-level Map has the same duplicate-instance hazard as any JavaScript registry - two copies of the package mean two Maps and unknown-token errors.
Calling resolve at module top level turns an unregistered token into an import-time crash for every consumer of that module; resolve inside functions, after the composition root has run.
